stances.claim: Yes, the Supreme Court disciplines justices and judges below itself -- through the Judicial Integrity Board, exercising its constitutional administrative-supervision power.
stances.rhetorical_move: direct Q&A opener with affirmative thesis

stances.claim: The JIB has 'vast and encompassing powers,' covering not only judges but also lawyers and judicial personnel including officers of the OCA, and even those in quasi-judicial bodies like the CSC and COA.
The JIB is the 'go-to' office for complaining about misconduct of justices, judges, lawyers, and judicial personnel nationwide.
The OCA's role has appropriately narrowed to court operations and well-being, leaving disciplinary functions to the JIB.
Private and low-profile JIB proceedings are appropriate to preserve the integrity of magistrates against groundless charges by defeated litigants, while final SC judgments are properly published.

Anonymous complaints being a viable pathway, referred to the Office of the General Counsel within 10 calendar days for evaluation and investigation.
Lawyers being disciplined under the JIB jurisdiction when their imputed acts also violate the Lawyer's Oath or Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability.

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to readers asking whether the Supreme Court also disciplines justices and judges below itself, Panganiban answers yes -- through its constitutional administrative-supervision power under Article VIII, Section 6, partly delegated to the Judicial Integrity Board (JIB), created on July 7, 2000 and headed by ret. Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez. (The JIB was renamed an 'Office' on April 22, 2025, but the change has not yet been implemented.) He explains the JIB's vast and encompassing reach: appellate justices of the CA, CTA, and Sandiganbayan; trial judges of the RTC, MTC, and Shari'ah Courts; lawyers as 'officers of the courts'; and judicial and quasi-judicial personnel including top OCA officials, the CSC, COA, Ombudsman, and DOJ as referring bodies. Disciplinary proceedings may be triggered motu proprio (by the SC or JIB based on records, media reports, or criminal convictions) or by interested persons through verified or substantiated anonymous complaints. He walks through the procedural ladder -- Complaints and Docket Services determines form-and-substance sufficiency, the respondent is given 10 calendar days to comment, the Office of the Executive Director submits a report within 15 days, the JIB resolves within 30 days, and the resolution goes to the Supreme Court for affirmation, modification, or reversal (usually affirmed). The OCA now handles court operations and may receive delegated investigations for less serious or light charges, completing them within 60 days. The JIB does its work privately and low-profile to shield magistrates from groundless complaints by defeated litigants, while the SC's final judgments are published online for public access.
